title: Checkpoint: Inside the Machine
objective: After this level you can explain how bits, gates, a processor and memory turn stored numbers into text, pictures and sums.
summary: The bytes 72, 73, 33 spell HI! as text and a shade of yellow as a pixel: context decides. Recap of bits, codes, gates, adders, the processor loop and memory.

cards.headline: 72, 73, 33. A word, a color or a sum?
cards.body: Chapter 1 finale. Every stop in this chapter turned something into numbers. Now take one short row of bytes and read it three ways, then ask who decides which reading is right.

items.label: Read as plain numbers
points: Sent through adders, they sum to 178

cards.headline: Who decides?
cards.body: The bits themselves don't say. Context does, such as the file's format: a text app reads those bytes through the ASCII codebook, while an image viewer reads them as red, green and blue. Even an instruction is only a binary pattern until the processor's decode step splits it into meaningful parts. Same bits, different reader, different meaning.

cards.headline: The whole chapter in one breath
cards.body: A bit is one yes-or-no. Eight make a byte, with 256 patterns. Codebooks like ASCII turn bytes into letters, while pixels and samples turn pictures and sound into numbers. Gates built from switches combine bits, and adders built from gates do sums. A processor fetches, decodes and executes instructions billions of times a second, fed through layers of memory from fast cache to roomy storage.

cards.headline: Chapter 1 complete
learned: How a computer turns text, pictures and sound into numbers, and why the same bytes can mean different things.
Why each extra bit doubles the patterns, and how bytes stack up from kilobytes to terabytes.
How AND, OR and NOT gates, wired into adders, add two binary numbers.
Why a processor loops through fetch, decode and execute, fed by layers of memory.

questions.prompt: Match each way of reading the bytes 72, 73, 33 with what you get.
questions.explanation: Read as ASCII text, the screen shows HI!. Read as one pixel, they're a shade of yellow. Read as plain numbers, they sum to 178.

questions.prompt: What decides whether a program shows the bytes 72, 73, 33 as HI! or as a shade of yellow?

options.label: The bits themselves carry a hidden label
options.rationale: The bits alone do not say what they mean.

options.label: Context, such as the file format
Whichever meaning has the bigger number
options.rationale: Both readings use exactly the same numbers.

options.label: The speed of the processor's clock
options.rationale: Clock speed paces work; it does not choose a meaning.

questions.explanation: Context, such as the file format, tells a program whether to read bytes as text, colors or numbers.

questions.prompt: In Level 8's decode step, what is an instruction before the processor splits it into parts?

options.label: A picture of the operation
options.rationale: Instructions are stored as numbers, like everything else.

options.label: A binary pattern, like any other data
A line of English text
options.rationale: The processor reads binary patterns, not English.

questions.explanation: An instruction is a binary pattern; decoding splits it into fields that each mean something.

questions.prompt: From Level 9: the layer of memory that is fast SRAM right on the processor chip is _____.

options.label: storage
options.rationale: Storage is the slowest, cheapest layer.

options.label: the program counter
options.rationale: That holds one address, not a layer of memory.

questions.explanation: Cache is fast SRAM, up to several megabytes, on the processor chip.

questions.prompt: From Level 4: what does Unicode give every character?

options.label: A unique number, on any platform
Its own font and color
options.rationale: Unicode assigns numbers; phones and apps choose the look.

options.label: A place on every keyboard
options.rationale: Most characters are not on a keyboard.

questions.explanation: Unicode gives every character a unique number, whatever the platform, program or language.
